nameStory: The Lapland longspur gets its name from two key features: 'Lapland' refers to the Arctic region of northern Scandinavia where these birds were first studied extensively, and 'longspur' describes the elongated hind claw that extends backward from their foot like a natural snowshoe. This extra-long toe claw helps them navigate across snow and grab onto vegetation in their harsh northern habitat.
description: The Lapland longspur is a sparrow-sized songbird that visits New England during migration and winter, escaping from its Arctic breeding grounds. These sturdy little birds are about the size of a house sparrow but with a more compact, rounded build suited for cold weather. Males in breeding plumage sport a distinctive black face and throat with a white stripe behind the eye, while females and winter birds are more subtly marked with streaky brown and buff coloring. They're ground-loving birds that prefer open areas where they can forage for seeds in flocks.

idTips.label: Long hind claw
idTips.description: Look for an unusually long, straight claw extending backward from the hind toe - much longer than typical sparrows and visible even at a distance when the bird is walking

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies in distinctive undulating waves with rapid wingbeats followed by brief closed-wing glides, often calling with musical twitter notes during flight

idTips.label: Ground behavior
idTips.description: Walks and runs on the ground rather than hopping like most sparrows, with a shuffling gait that keeps them low to search for seeds

idTips.label: Rusty wing patches
idTips.description: Shows warm chestnut or rusty-colored patches on the wings that are visible when folded and especially noticeable in flight

idTips.label: White outer tail feathers
idTips.description: Flashes bright white outer tail feathers when taking off or landing, creating a distinctive flickering pattern against darker center tail feathers

idTips.label: Flock behavior
idTips.description: Almost always seen in flocks during New England visits, often mixing with snow buntings and horned larks in open areas

habitat: Look for Lapland longspurs in wide open spaces like airports, large agricultural fields, coastal dunes, and short-grass areas near the shore. They prefer areas with sparse, low vegetation where they can easily walk on the ground to forage for seeds. These birds avoid wooded areas and dense brush, sticking to expansive open terrain similar to their Arctic tundra breeding grounds.

seasonality.spring: Migrating flocks pass through from late March to early May, with males beginning to show their striking black and white breeding plumage. Listen for their musical flight calls as flocks move northward.
seasonality.summer: Absent from New England as they're busy breeding on the Arctic tundra far to the north. Any longspur sighting in summer would be extremely rare.
seasonality.fall: Fall migrants arrive from late September through November, mostly in drab winter plumage that can make identification challenging. Peak numbers usually occur in October.
seasonality.winter: Small numbers may linger through winter in coastal areas and large open fields, often associating with snow bunting flocks. Their rusty wing patches and long hind claws remain the best identification features.

funFact: Lapland longspurs travel some of the longest migration routes of any songbird, with some individuals flying over 4,000 miles from their Arctic breeding grounds to wintering areas - that's like flying from Maine to Alaska twice a year!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with snow buntings, but longspurs walk on the ground instead of hopping, lack the snow bunting's extensive white wing patches, and have that distinctive long hind claw. Remember: 'Longspurs walk, buntings hop' - and you can often see that long back toe even from a distance.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'longspurs,' these birds are not related to true spurs or game birds - the name simply describes their elongated hind toe claw. They were formerly classified with sparrows and buntings but are now in their own family due to genetic studies showing they're more closely related to thick-billed longspur and snow bunting.
compareHints: The Lapland longspur is the only member of its genus regularly seen in New England, making it unique among the typical longspurs. Compared to its closest relative here, the snow bunting, Lapland longspurs are smaller, lack extensive white wing markings, show more rusty-brown coloring, and have that characteristic walking gait with the obvious long hind claw. Snow buntings are chunkier, whiter overall, and hop rather than walk.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the more likely Lapland longspur, chestnut-collared longspurs are smaller and more compact, with that distinctive chestnut collar in breeding males versus the Lapland's black throat and face markings.
Compared to the more common Lapland Longspur, Smith's Longspur shows warmer buff and rust tones rather than black and white contrasts, and lacks the white wing patches visible in flight.
